criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural and small-town drinking water service access, infrastructure functionality, service reliability, crowding, and daily basic water access (>=20 litres per person per day) in Akatsi (North and South) and East Gonja districts in Ghana.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines decentralized rural water governance under the Community Ownership and Management (COM) model, District Assembly planning/budgeting, and administrative monitoring (DiMES). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyses tariff and cost-recovery rules (comparing monthly levies, volumetric pay-as-you-fetch tariffs, and no-fixed-tariff/post-failure mobilization regimes against borehole functionality and revenue adequacy), statutory/bye-law reserve rules (national model bye-law MLGRDE 2008 requiring WSMTs to deposit >=20% of net monthly revenue into capital accounts), CWSA Facility Management Plan rules, and lack of enforcement of the CWSA Legislative Instrument (2007) governing unplanned donor borehole construction.
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods empirical study combining reanalysis of a quantitative dataset (371 handpumps and 160 Water and Sanitation Management Teams mapped Nov 2011-Jan 2012) with primary field data collected Feb-Mar 2013 (21 key informant interviews, 7 site visits, 8 focus group discussions, and inspection of financial/administrative records and district budgets).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service access outcomes: borehole/handpump and small-town piped system functionality rates (including functionality stratified by tariff regime in Table 2: 74% monthly levy, 69% pay-as-you-fetch, 50% no fixed tariff), reliability (>18 days breakdown/year), basic service level compliance, proportion failing basic access of >=20 L/person/day, and tariff affordability.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (rural communities, WSMTs, and 371 handpumps/piped systems in Akatsi and East Gonja districts), exposure (tariff/cost-recovery regimes, bye-law capital reserve and budgeting rules, periodic maintenance, and COM governance/enforcement), outcome (functionality, reliability, basic water access, affordability), and mixed-methods observational case study design are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: These factors have had an impact on water consumption with 39% of residents in East Gonja and 49% of residents in Akatsi South and North failing to get basic access of at least 20 litres of water per person per day, according to Adank et al. (2013).

According to the national model bye-law, (MLGRDE, 2008) Water and Sanitation Management Teams for small towns are required to make a monthly payment of not less than 20% of their net monthly revenue to their capital account.
Two key and interrelated factors are identified: (1) tariff structure implemented by the community; (2) the routine maintenance of the infrastructure.
Firstly, we reanalysed existing quantitative datasets on water infrastructure and services for Akatsi South and North and East Gonja Districts.

Thirdly, we collected primary data from the two districts in 2013. Data collection included inspection and observation of water facilities, inspection of financial and administrative records (at the district or community/Water and Sanitation Management Team level).

raw_response.exposure: Tariff and cost-recovery rules (monthly levy vs. volumetric pay-as-you-fetch vs. no fixed tariff / post-failure mobilization; compliance with national model bye-law 20% capital account rule and OpEx/CapManEx budgeting), periodic maintenance regimes, and decentralized Community Ownership and Management (COM) regulatory/administrative governance (CWSA guidelines, DiMES monitoring, and enforcement of CWSA Legislative Instrument 2007).
raw_response.outcome: Borehole/handpump and small-town piped scheme functionality rates, service reliability (breakdowns exceeding 18 days/year), CWSA basic service level attainment, share of residents receiving basic access (>=20 L/person/day), and tariff affordability.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural communities and small towns in Akatsi (North and South) and East Gonja districts, Ghana: quantitative dataset of 371 handpumps (n = 253 in tariff/maintenance subgroup comparisons) and 160 Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs), plus 21 semi-structured key informant interviews, 7 site visits, and 8 focus group discussions.
raw_response.rationale: Full-text mixed-methods empirical study in rural Ghana satisfying all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope of Criterion 2. Beyond physical asset maintenance, the study empirically evaluates tariff and cost-recovery rules (comparing monthly levies, pay-as-you-fetch volumetric tariffs, and no-fixed-tariff post-failure collection on handpump functionality in Table 2, plus revenue sufficiency and affordability in Table 1), compliance with the national model bye-law capital reserve requirement, district composite budgeting rules, and enforcement of the CWSA Legislative Instrument (2007) in relation to water point functionality, reliability, and basic household water access.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods observational case study (quantitative cross-sectional survey reanalysis combined with qualitative key informant interviews, focus groups, site visits, and administrative/financial record review)
